exercises.prompt: The water held in a trap that blocks foul air is called the water ___.
exercises.hint: It seals the pipe from the room.
exercises.explanation: Without a seal, the stack talks to the room.

exercises.prompt: You are asked to clear a blocked soil stack with raw chemical while tenants are on the highest floor with open traps. You should:
exercises.explanation: Caustic plus acid plus methane is how plumbers get hurt. Method and PPE.

options.text: Protect people, use mechanical clearing as trained, and never mix unknown chemicals
Open the drinking tank into the stack
Ignore PPE because it is only waste

lessons.title: Vapour-compression cycle and components
lessons.briefing:
Almost every fridge and split AC you service uses the vapour-compression cycle. The compressor raises pressure and temperature of the vapour. The condenser rejects heat so the refrigerant becomes liquid. The expansion device (capillary or TXV) drops pressure. The evaporator absorbs heat as liquid boils at low pressure. If you cannot point to those four on a domestic fridge, you are not diagnosing — you are guessing.

High-side vs low-side: gauges, pipe temperatures, and frost patterns tell a story. Ice on the evaporator with a warm cabinet can be airflow, defrost, or charge — not “always add gas”. The thermostat stops the compressor; it does not fix a leak.

Electrical isolation still applies: unplug, discharge capacitors as trained, and do not short a thermostat with a nail to “test cooling”.
lessons.briefingSw: Compressor inainua shinikizo. Condenser inatoa joto. Expansion inashusha shinikizo. Evaporator inachukua joto. Usiweke gesi bila kuelewa mzunguko. Zima umeme kabla ya kufungua unit.

exercises.prompt: Which component raises refrigerant pressure and temperature?
exercises.explanation: The compressor compresses vapour; the condenser then rejects heat.

exercises.prompt: Heat is rejected to the room (or outside air) mainly at the:
exercises.explanation: Condenser heat rejection is why the back of a fridge is warm.

exercises.prompt: A capillary tube is a type of:
exercises.hint: It meters liquid to the evaporator.
exercises.explanation: Restriction drops pressure so boiling can happen in the evaporator.

exercises.prompt: To service a packaged unit electrically you first:
exercises.explanation: Capacitors store charge. Isolation is not optional.

options.text: Isolate power and prove dead as for any appliance
Hold the live to feel current
Ground the compressor shell to the water pipe randomly

exercises.prompt: The component that absorbs heat from the cabinet as refrigerant boils is the ___.
exercises.hint: It is the cold heat exchanger.
exercises.explanation: No airflow over a dirty evaporator means poor cooling even with a full charge.

exercises.prompt: A fridge ices heavily at the back wall but the cabinet is warm. A trainee reaches for a gas cylinder. What should happen?
exercises.explanation: Blind topping-up hides leaks and overcharges. Diagnose first.

options.text: Add gas until the pipe sweats
Check airflow, defrost, leaks, and evidence before any charge

lessons.title: Refrigerant law, recovery, and nitrogen
lessons.titleSw: Sheria ya gesi, recovery, na nitrogen
lessons.briefing:
Venting refrigerant to air is environmentally harmful and may be illegal. Recover into a proper cylinder with recovery equipment. Label cylinders. Mixing refrigerants in one bottle is a later technician’s nightmare.

Pressure tests use dry nitrogen, never oxygen or compressed air from an oily workshop compressor. Oxygen plus oil in a system is an explosion risk. Use a regulator and know the test pressure from the manufacturer — do not “pump until it feels hard”.

Goggles and gloves when opening systems. Liquid refrigerant on skin is a freeze burn. Evacuate to the required vacuum before charging; moisture plus refrigerant plus oil makes acids and sludge.

SDS and cylinder colours: know what is in your hand. R600a (isobutane) in many domestic fridges is flammable — no smoking, no sparks, follow hydrocarbon procedures.
lessons.briefingSw: Usitoe gesi hewani — fanya recovery. Jaribu shinikizo kwa nitrogen, si oxygen. Vacuum kabla ya charge. R600a ni kuwaka; fuata taratibu za hydrocarbon.

exercises.prompt: Why recover refrigerant instead of releasing it?
exercises.explanation: Recovery is competent RAC practice, not optional kindness.

options.text: Legal and environmental duty — many refrigerants harm climate and may be illegal to vent
It makes ice cream freeze faster
NITA requires open vents for luck

exercises.prompt: Systems should be strength/leak tested with:
exercises.explanation: Oxygen + oil is dangerous. Moisture in air is also unwelcome.

options.text: Workshop air from an oily compressor

exercises.prompt: R600a in domestic cabinets is a concern because it is:
exercises.explanation: Treat HC systems as flammable. Charge masses are small but ignition is real.

options.text: A hydrocarbon — flammable; needs spark-aware procedure

exercises.prompt: A deep vacuum before charging is mainly to:
exercises.explanation: Air raises head pressure; moisture damages the system chemically.

exercises.prompt: Putting used refrigerant into a recovery cylinder instead of the atmosphere is called ___.
exercises.explanation: Recovery, recycle, reclaim — know which your equipment actually does.

exercises.prompt: A trainee wants to find a leak with a cigarette lighter on a hydrocarbon fridge. Your response?
exercises.explanation: Electronic or bubble methods, not naked flames on HC systems.

options.text: Stop immediately; use approved leak detection, isolate ignition, follow HC rules
Open all windows and still use the lighter
Add oxygen to make the flame clearer

lessons.title: Leak, charge, and performance checks
lessons.briefing:
Charge is a measured quantity, often by mass (weigh-in) on a capillary system, or by superheat/subcooling on TXV systems as you are taught. “Until the pipe ices” is not a method. Find and repair leaks, replace driers when the system has been open, evacuate, then charge.

Airflow is half of refrigeration. A blocked condenser (dust, cow hair, butcher-shop grease) raises head pressure and trips overloads. A blocked evaporator ices. Clean, straighten fins, check fans, then talk about gas.

After service: cabinet temperature vs spec, no abnormal noise, no ice where it should not be, electrical covers back, and a record of refrigerant type and mass. That record is professional, and it protects the next person.
lessons.briefingSw: Charge ni uzito au superheat/subcooling, si “hadi barafu”. Rekodi uvujaji. Safisha condenser na evaporator. Weka kumbukumbu ya aina na kiasi cha gesi.

exercises.prompt: The professional way to charge many capillary domestic systems is:
exercises.explanation: Overcharge is as bad as undercharge.

options.text: Weigh in the specified mass after vacuum
Fill until the compressor is silent

exercises.prompt: A filthy condenser typically causes:
exercises.explanation: Clean heat exchangers before you condemn compressors.

options.text: High head pressure and poor cooling / trips
Freezing of the compressor oil into ice cubes

exercises.prompt: After opening a system you often replace the:
exercises.explanation: Driers are cheap compared with acid and burnout.

exercises.prompt: Service records should include:
exercises.explanation: The next technician and the law both like records.

options.text: Refrigerant type, quantity, and work done

exercises.prompt: Charging by reading a scale under the cylinder is called a ___-in charge.
exercises.explanation: Weigh-in is standard on many factory-charged capillary units.

exercises.prompt: Split AC cools one room weakly. Outdoor unit is packed with lint. Trainee wants to add 2 kg of mixed leftover gas. What do you do?
exercises.explanation: Mixed leftovers are not a refrigerant. Dirty condensers fake a “low gas” story.

options.text: Clean airflow path, confirm type, leak-check, then charge only the specified refrigerant to spec
Swap indoor and outdoor pipes randomly

lessons.title: Seams, pressing, and assembly order
lessons.titleSw: Mishono, pressing, na mpangilio wa kushona
lessons.briefing:
Construction is a sequence, not a pile of random seams. A typical shirt or uniform blouse: shoulder seams, attach collar or neck facing, set sleeves (or join side seams then sleeves, depending on the method), then cuffs, then hem. If you hem first you often cannot set a sleeve. Write the order on your job card the way the assessor expects.

Plain seams are sewn, pressed open, then neatened with zigzag, overlocker, or a turned edge as specified. Underpress every seam before you cross it with another. “Sew it all then iron at the end” is how collars twist and seam allowances get trapped. Use the ham and sleeve board for curves; do not crush a puff sleeve flat on the big board.

Clip inward curves and notch outward curves so they lie. Grade bulky seams (collar, waistband) so layers form a stair, not a ridge. For zips, a centred zip needs a basted opening, the zip face-down, and stitching an even distance from the teeth. Test on a scrap if the fabric is slippery.

Quality at this stage: even seam width, matching notches, no puckers, and thread ends finished. Assessors put a ruler on your 1.5 cm — they are not guessing.
lessons.briefingSw: Fuata mpangilio: mabega, shingo, mikono, kisha hem. Press kila mshono kabla ya kuuvuka. Neatisha kwa zigzag au overlocker. Clip curves. Zip inahitaji basting. Upana wa mshono lazima uwe sawa — wakaguzi hupima.

exercises.prompt: Why underpress a seam before crossing it with another seam?
exercises.hint: Bulk in a junction cannot be pressed out later.
exercises.explanation: Each seam is a foundation for the next. This is a scored finishing behaviour.

options.text: So allowances lie flat and the next seam is accurate
Pressing is only for the shop window

exercises.prompt: Notching an outward curve (e.g. a collar point area or convex seam) is done to:
exercises.hint: Extra fabric in a curve has nowhere to go.
exercises.explanation: Clips on concave, notches on convex — both help the seam allowance sit after turning.

options.text: Remove bulk so the curve turns without a ridge

exercises.prompt: A professional open (plain) seam is usually:
exercises.hint: Open and neatened is the default woven method.
exercises.explanation: Unless the spec says French or overlocked-together, press open and neaten both edges.

options.text: Sewn, pressed to one side untrimmed always
Sewn at the planned allowance, pressed open, then neatened

exercises.prompt: Why is assembly order written on a job card?
exercises.hint: Some operations are impossible after a hem or a closed side seam.
exercises.explanation: Planning is part of competence, not extra theory.

options.text: So sleeves, collars, and closures are attached while the garment can still be opened flat

exercises.prompt: Trimming layered seam allowances to different widths so they stack without a ridge is called seam ___.
exercises.explanation: Grading reduces bulk in collars, cuffs, and waistbands.

exercises.prompt: You set a sleeve and the ease forms one big pleat at the cap. The spec is a smooth head. What do you do?
exercises.hint: Ease is tiny fullness, not a tuck.
exercises.explanation: Two rows of ease stitching, steam, and even distribution are the textbook fix. A pleat is a construction fault on a plain sleeve.

options.text: Leave it; ease always looks like a pleat
Unpick, redistribute ease with two rows of gather stitches, shrink with the iron if the cloth allows, and restitch
Cut a dart out of the cap
Glue the cap to the dummy

lessons.title: Fitting, hems, and quality control
lessons.titleSw: Fitting, hem, na udhibiti wa ubora
lessons.briefing:
Fitting is a measured process. Put the garment on the client or dummy, pin on the right side, and mark with chalk. Do not cut until you have recorded the change on the pattern or a fitting sheet. A skirt that is 4 cm too long is not “trimmed at the floor”. Unpick the hem, measure from the waist with a stick or metre, mark a level hem, then rebuild the planned hem allowance (often 3–4 cm double-fold on uniforms).

Closures must work: buttons align with holes, zippers open fully, hook-and-bar takes strain off a waist zip. Buttonholes are cut after stitching, not before, unless you use a bound method that requires a window. Secure buttons with a shank on coats so the fabric can sit.

Final press is directional: seams the way they were sewn, collars rolled at the edge, hems without a second shine-line from a dirty iron. Hang the garment and walk around it: unmatched side seams, twisted legs, and hanging threads fail assessment even if the design is pretty.

Before you submit, use a QC list: measurements vs spec, symmetry, inside neatness, labels if required, and safety (no pins left in). That list is how industry and CDACC both think.
lessons.briefingSw: Fitting ni kipimo, si kukata ovyo. Rekodi mabadiliko. Hem ndefu inarekebishwa kwa kufungua na kupima kutoka kiunoni. Angalia zip, vifungo, na symmetry. Fanya orodha ya QC kabla ya kuwasilisha.

exercises.prompt: A double-fold hem is 4 cm too long. The professional fix is:
exercises.explanation: Length comes from a measured mark. Guess-cutting destroys the finish and the allowance for next term.

options.text: Cut the hem off at floor level with scissors
Unpick, re-measure from a fixed point (waist/dummy), and resew the planned hem allowance

exercises.prompt: Why make a button shank on a thick coat?
exercises.hint: Thickness needs space under the button.
exercises.explanation: A tight-sewn button on a coat pulls and the hole never meets.

options.text: So the button sits above the cloth thickness and the hole can close without strain

exercises.prompt: Which item belongs on a final QC list?
exercises.explanation: Quality is evidence against a spec, not a feeling.

options.text: Whether the trainee likes the colour
Measurements against the spec, symmetry, threads, and no pins left in

exercises.prompt: Fitting pins should be placed:
exercises.hint: The dummy is not the pattern.
exercises.explanation: Transfer marks. Cutting on the person is unsafe and inaccurate.

options.text: On the wrong side only so the client cannot see errors
On the body, marking the correction, then transferred to cloth/pattern before cutting

exercises.prompt: The extra length of cloth turned up at the bottom of a skirt or trouser is the ___ allowance.
exercises.explanation: Hem allowance is planned in the pattern. It is not leftover waste.

exercises.prompt: An assessor finds three pins still in a finished uniform and a hanging bobbin thread at the zip. Result?
exercises.explanation: Pins in a garment are a safety fail. Loose threads are a quality fail. Both are easy marks lost.

options.text: Ignore — pins are a design feature
Those are finishing faults; remove pins, tidy threads, and only then present

lessons.title: Week 9 — Gents wear: shirt, trouser, and fly
lessons.briefing:
Gents wear is a distinct core in fashion L5 (shirts, trousers, sometimes a jacket). A man’s shirt: yoke, collar and stand, placket, cuff with placket, and extra length at the back. Collar points must match; the stand sits so the collar rolls, not flaps. Interfacing in collar and stand is not optional if the spec is a uniform shirt.

Trousers: front crease on the grain, fly with zip guard, waistband with a curtain or facing, and pockets that do not gape. Rise (body rise) is measured seated as well as standing or the crotch will cut. A ladies’ block is not a gents’ block — different balance and fly construction.

Topstitching on a shirt is a quality mark: even width, matching thread, no tunnels. Buttons: men’s shirts traditionally button left over right (as worn). Confirm the college spec. Sleeve pitch: the sleeve cap notch matches the shoulder; twisting sleeves are a setting error from construction week, still assessed here.

Assessed sample: a school/office shirt or a pair of trousers with a working fly. Attach the spec sheet. Industrial attachment later will expect you to hit minutes-per-operation; here you hit quality first.
lessons.briefingSw: Shati: yoke, collar na stand, placket, cuff. Suruali: crease, fly, waistband, rise. Block ya wanawake si ya wanaume. Topstitch sawa. Interfacing kwenye collar.

exercises.prompt: A shirt collar that will not sit is often missing:
exercises.explanation: The stand is the engineered piece. Skipping it on a formal shirt is a fail.

options.text: A correctly interfaced stand and balanced collar points

exercises.prompt: Trouser fly construction must include:
exercises.explanation: A fly without a guard or bar-tack fails first wash.

options.text: Zip, guard/facing, and bar-tacks at stress points as specified

exercises.prompt: If the crotch bites when the learner sits, check:
exercises.explanation: Gents trousers fail on rise more than on hem length.

options.text: Body rise / crotch depth on the pattern

exercises.prompt: Shirt back yokes exist to:
exercises.explanation: A well-set yoke is a gents-wear competence.

options.text: Add structure and often conceal a shoulder split / hanging loop area

exercises.prompt: The band that lifts a shirt collar off the neck is the collar ___.
exercises.explanation: Collar and stand are two pattern pieces plus interfacing.

exercises.prompt: Gents school trousers twist so the crease spirals. Trainee says “press harder”. Diagnosis?
exercises.explanation: Gents wear still obeys warp and weft. Pressing is not a grain correction.

options.text: Legs off grain or twisted in making — recut/rehang on grain; pressing will not hold a grain fault

lessons.title: Week 7 — Pattern grading and size sets
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 7 — Grading ya pattern na saizi
lessons.briefing:
Construction of a master pattern (size 12 or the college block) is not the end. Grading produces the size set (e.g. 8–16) using grade rules: how much the bust, waist, hip, and length change per size. You do not photocopy at 110% — that enlarges buttons, seam allowances, and dart intake wrongly. Shift cardinal points: bust point, waist, hip, shoulder, scye, hem.

Manual grading uses a grade table and tracks (move X and Y). Computer grading does the same with CAD. Nested patterns should look like a family: even gaps at side seams, not a fan that explodes at the hem only. Check that dart tips still aim at the bust point after grade.

Kenyan school uniforms often have a size chart in centimetres. Measure a sample of learners; do not import a European chart blindly. Ease must remain after grading — a size 16 that lost wearing ease is unwearable.

This week: grade a skirt block one size up and one down, nest them, and measure hip circumference against the chart. That is the CDACC grading outcome.
lessons.briefingSw: Grading si photocopy 110%. Tumia grade rules: bust, waist, hip, urefu. Cardinal points. Nested patterns ziwe familia. Ease ibaki. Pima chati ya Kenya, si ya Ulaya tu.

exercises.prompt: Photocopying a pattern at 115% is a poor grade because it:
exercises.explanation: Grade rules move body measurements; SA often stays 1.5 cm.

options.text: Also scales seam allowances, buttonholes, and dart logic incorrectly

exercises.prompt: A nested set that fans wildly only at the hem usually means:
exercises.explanation: Inspect the nest before you cut a size run.

exercises.prompt: Wearing ease after grading should:
exercises.explanation: Size 16 is not size 12 with no ease and longer hem only.

options.text: Disappear on larger sizes to save cloth
Remain as specified so the garment can be worn

exercises.prompt: Cardinal points in grading include:
exercises.explanation: Those points get X/Y moves from the grade table.

options.text: Bust, waist, hip, shoulder, armhole, hem

exercises.prompt: The table of millimetre moves per size for each landmark is a ___ rule table.
exercises.explanation: Without a table you are guessing, not grading.

exercises.prompt: Size 10 blouse fits. Size 16 made by scaling the whole block including 1.5 cm SA to 2.2 cm and huge darts. Fix?
exercises.explanation: That is the difference between grading and enlarging a drawing.

options.text: Re-grade with constant SA and proper bust/waist/hip rules; true the darts
Only lengthen the hem by 40 cm

lessons.title: Week 8 — Ladies wear: dart, ease, and closures
lessons.briefing:
Ladies wear units in Kenyan fashion L5 typically produce a blouse, dress, or skirt that proves dart manipulation, closures, and fit on a female form. Bust darts point toward the bust point and stop short (about 1.5–2.5 cm) so they do not sit as cones on the apex. Waist darts shape the torso. If the client is between sizes, you alter the pattern — you do not guess on the cloth.

Closures: centred zip, lapped zip, invisible zip, or buttons and placket. Invisible zips need the right foot and to be stitched close to the coils. A gaping back neck is a pattern/shoulder issue, not a bigger zip. Facings and bias bindings neat on the inside are marked hard.

Ease: a woven blouse needs wearing ease at bust (often ~5–8 cm depending on style). A “body-con” woven without stretch and without ease will not button. Knit ladies wear follows the textile week: stretch stitches, stay tape at the shoulder.

Assessed sample: a school or office blouse with collar or neck finish, set-in sleeve, buttoned front or zip, and a finished hem. QC against the spec from sketching week.

exercises.explanation: Dart intake shapes to the apex but the tip fades before it.

options.text: Creates a pointy cone — stop the dart short of the apex

exercises.prompt: An invisible zip that shows teeth usually means:
exercises.explanation: Practice on scrap of the same fabric and zip length.

options.text: Stitching too far from the coils or the wrong foot

exercises.hint: Not skin-tight unless stretch/style says so.
exercises.explanation: Measure body + ease = garment circumference on the spec.

options.text: Extra circumference so the wearer can breathe and move

exercises.prompt: A gaping back neck is usually fixed by:
exercises.explanation: Ladies wear is a fitting unit as much as a sewing unit.

options.text: Pattern alteration at neck/shoulder, not by pulling the zip harder

exercises.prompt: The fullest bust landmark that darts aim toward is the bust ___.
exercises.explanation: Measure BP height from the shoulder; it changes with size and age.

exercises.prompt: Buttons strain and gap on a woven blouse even though hip and waist are fine. First pattern action?
exercises.explanation: Ladies wear fails at the bust more than at the hem. Measure.

options.text: Add bust ease or a dart/fullness alteration; check bust circumference vs body + ease

lessons.title: Lockstitch machine and workshop safety
lessons.briefing:
Fashion practicals start at the table, not at the pattern. Unplug the iron when you leave the board. Cover the needle, and never sew with the presser foot up. A lockstitch machine forms a stitch when the needle thread loops around the bobbin thread. If the machine is threaded wrong — especially missing the take-up lever — you get bird’s nests, skipped stitches, or a jammed hook.

Needle size must match fabric: 70/10 or 80/12 for shirting, 90/14 or 100/16 for denim and canvas. A blunt or bent needle on heavy cloth is the usual cause of skipped stitches, not “the machine is old”. Stitch length is typically 2.0–2.5 mm for construction seams and longer for basting. Tension discs must be closed when you thread; the thread sits between them, not on top.

Bobbin winding should be even. Drop the bobbin so it rotates the way the machine manual shows, pull the thread through the slot, and hold both threads to the back before the first stitch. At the end of a seam, reverse two or three stitches, then cut threads with the thread cutter or snips — not by yanking the garment.

CDACC/NITA assessors watch whether you can thread independently, sew a straight seam on calico, and leave the station safe. That is the first unit, before any fashion drawing.
lessons.briefingSw: Anza na usalama: zima pasi, funika sindano. Lockstitch inahitaji uzi wa needle na bobbin kukutana. Chagua sindano kulingana na kitambaa: 80/12 kwa shirting, 90/14 au 100/16 kwa denim. Tension na take-up lever ni muhimu. Kadiria stitch 2.0–2.5 mm. Wakaguzi wanatazama kama unaweza kushona mshono sawa na kuacha meza salama.

exercises.hint: Play or watch the demonstration, then confirm.
exercises.explanation: You confirmed that the demonstration was completed.

exercises.hint: Skipped stitches are mechanical, not decorative.
exercises.explanation: Heavy fabric needs a larger, sharp needle, a complete thread path through the take-up, and balanced tension.

options.text: Needle size and condition, threading path, and tension discs

exercises.hint: Tension is not applied with the foot up on most lockstitch machines.
exercises.explanation: Sewing with the foot up gives loops, poor feed, and broken needles.

exercises.explanation: About 2–2.5 mm (roughly 10–12 SPI) is standard. Tiny stitches perforate; huge stitches look homemade and weak.

exercises.hint: Small metal or plastic spool under the needle plate.
exercises.explanation: Needle thread and bobbin thread lock in the fabric. Wrong bobbin insertion causes loops underneath.

exercises.explanation: Underside looping is the classic “top thread not in tension / missed take-up” fault. Re-thread with the foot up, then down, and test on scrap.

lessons.title: Pattern, grain, and cutting
lessons.briefing:
A garment is decided on the table before a single stitch. Patterns carry grainlines, notches, drill holes, size, and cutting instructions. The grainline must sit parallel to the selvedge (or to the warp on a folded length). Off-grain collars twist; off-grain trousers twist around the leg.

Standard woven seam allowance in many TVET practicals is 1.5 cm (sometimes 1 cm on necklines after staystitching — follow the pattern). Hem allowances are larger and must be planned, not guessed at the floor. Fold fabric right sides together unless the lay plan says otherwise. Pin inside the allowance, not on the stitch line, and cut with the shears resting on the table — don’t lift the cloth and chew it in the air.

Notches match pieces: one notch often means a front, two a back, or they mark ease. Transfer markings with tailor’s tacks, chalk, or a tracing wheel as taught. Staystitch curved necks and armholes 5 mm from the edge, in the direction that stops stretch, before you handle the piece a lot.

Assessors look at a clean lay: little waste, all pieces facing the planned nap/print direction, and no missing facings. Count pieces against the pattern chart before you move the waste.
lessons.briefingSw: Grainline inafaa kuwa sambamba na selvedge. Seam allowance ya kawaida ni 1.5 cm. Kata kitambaa mezani, si hewani. Notches zinalinganisha vipande. Staystitch shingo kabla ya kushughulikia. Hesabu vipande kulingana na chart kabla ya kutupa waste.

exercises.prompt: What is the usual seam allowance for most woven garments in TVET practicals?
exercises.hint: About a finger joint, not a hem.
exercises.explanation: 1.5 cm is the common woven construction allowance before fitting changes.

exercises.prompt: If a grainline is not parallel to the selvedge, the garment may:
exercises.hint: Fabric wants to return to true grain.
exercises.explanation: Off-grain cutting is a classic cause of twisting trousers, rolling hems, and collars that will not sit.

options.text: Twist or hang crooked after pressing

exercises.prompt: Staystitching on a neckline is done to:
exercises.explanation: A row of stitching just inside the seam line keeps the neck the drafted size.

options.text: Stabilise a bias or curved edge so it does not stretch before joining

exercises.prompt: Why pin inside the seam allowance rather than through the stitch line?
exercises.hint: The needle should not fight metal on the stitch path if you can avoid it.
exercises.explanation: Many trainers require pins removed as you sew. Never sew over a pin if the rule is “remove as you go”.

lessons.title: Week 6 — Fashion sketching and specifications
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 6 — Mchoro wa fashion na spec
lessons.briefing:
CDACC fashion includes sketching figures and producing working drawings. A croquis is a proportioned template (often 8–9 heads for fashion, more realistic for school uniforms). Design sketches show silhouette, style lines, and fabric suggestion. They are not the same as a technical flat: flats are 2D, garment as if laid on a table, seams and topstitching visible, left and right consistent.

A spec sheet / working drawing carries measurements (bust, waist, hip, length, sleeve, hem depth, seam allowance), stitch types, notions (zip length, button size), and fabric. Without it the machinist invents, and the assessor cannot mark against a standard. Callouts: “lockstitch 2.4 mm, 1.5 cm SA, 20 cm invisible zip”.

Shade for drape, but do not hide construction. Front and back views. If there is a lining, show it. Kenyan polytechnic practicals often ask for a school skirt or shirt — draw the actual garment, not a Paris gown, unless the brief says otherwise.

Portfolio this week: one croquis illustration plus one flat plus a measurement table for a ladies’ blouse. That is how industry hands work to the sewing line.
lessons.briefingSw: Croquis ni kielelezo cha mwili. Flat ni mchoro wa kiufundi wa nguo. Spec sheet ina vipimo, stitch, zip, na kitambaa. Chora mbele na nyuma. Sare ya shule ni mradi halali.

exercises.explanation: Illustration sells; flats instruct. You need both in the unit.

options.text: A 2D working drawing of the garment with seams, topstitch, and callouts

exercises.prompt: Seam allowance belongs:
exercises.explanation: 1.5 cm is common for garments but must be written.

options.text: On the spec/pattern, stated in millimetres or centimetres

exercises.explanation: A princess line that vanishes at the side is a drawing error.

lessons.title: Week 5 — Textile science and fabric choice
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 5 — Sayansi ya nguo na chaguo la kitambaa
lessons.briefing:
Fashion Level 5 occupational standards start with textile principles, not only the machine. Fibres are natural (cotton, linen, wool, silk) or manufactured (polyester, nylon, viscose, blends). Cotton breathes and sews easily; it wrinkles and shrinks if not pre-shrunk. Wool felts with heat and moisture. Polyester is strong and crease-resistant but melts under a too-hot iron — that is why you test the iron on a scrap.

Yarn becomes fabric by weaving (plain, twill, satin) or knitting. Woven fabrics have warp (along the grain, little stretch) and weft. Knit fabrics stretch and need ball-point needles, stretch stitches, and a walking foot or careful feed. Cutting a woven shirt on the bias (45°) gives drape; cutting off-grain makes a hem twist after washing — a classic assessor fail.

Grainline on the pattern must follow the warp unless the designer marked bias. Selvage is the factory edge parallel to warp. Nap (velvet, corduroy) must all lie the same way or light hits as two colours. Pre-wash or steam-shrink as the fabric requires before you cut a uniform that must survive the hostel laundry.

Identify: fibre burn tests are taught with care (tiny sample, ventilation, never in a sewing classroom full of cloth). Care labels: wash temperature, tumble, iron dots. Portfolio: a fabric swatch card with fibre, weave, suitable garment, needle size, and stitch length.
lessons.briefingSw: Nyuzi asilia dhidi ya synthetic. Cotton inapumua na kuwa wrinkles; polyester inayeyuka kwa pasi moto. Weave ina warp na weft; knit inanyooshwa. Grainline ifuate warp. Pre-shrink sare. Nap ya velvet iwe upande mmoja.

exercises.prompt: Warp yarns in a woven fabric generally:
exercises.explanation: Weft is across. Grainline of most shirts follows warp.

options.text: Run across the fabric and stretch a lot
Run parallel to the selvage and have little stretch

exercises.prompt: A polyester school blouse should be pressed:
exercises.explanation: Shine and holes are heat damage. Use a press cloth.

options.text: On linen heat with steam forever
On a cooler setting, tested on a scrap — synthetics melt

exercises.prompt: Knit jersey for a T-shirt needs:
exercises.explanation: Sharp needles cut knits and cause holes that run.

options.text: A leather needle and 4 mm straight stitch only
Ball-point or stretch needle and a stretch stitch or overlocker

exercises.prompt: Nap fabrics such as corduroy must be cut:
exercises.explanation: One panel will look a different shade if the pile is reversed.

options.text: With pile running in mixed directions to save cloth
With all pieces in the same pile direction

exercises.prompt: The factory-finished edge of woven cloth parallel to the warp is the ___.
exercises.explanation: Grainline is usually parallel to the selvage.

exercises.prompt: You cut a cotton uniform without pre-washing. After hostel laundry it is two sizes smaller. Cause?
exercises.explanation: CDACC textile principles exist so the garment still fits after wet treatment.

options.text: Relaxation/residual shrinkage — pre-shrink cottons before cutting production garments

lessons.title: Week 2 — DC safety, batteries, commissioning, and maintenance
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 2 — Usalama wa DC, betri, commissioning
lessons.briefing:
Solar DC arcs do not pass through zero like AC and can persist. Cover modules or isolate strings using rated devices before working. Use DC-rated isolators, fuses, connectors, and cable. Never mix incompatible “MC4-style” brands unless the manufacturer approves them. Crimp with the correct tool and pull-test.

Batteries store dangerous energy. Match chemistry and BMS settings; fuse close to the positive terminal; ventilate lead-acid banks; keep lithium batteries within manufacturer temperature limits. Torque lugs to specification and record it. Commission in the manufacturer’s order: polarity, insulation where required, open-circuit voltage, battery voltage, inverter settings, controlled load test, and monitoring.

Handover includes shutdown/startup, expected daily limits, cleaning without standing on panels, and an emergency contact. Maintenance compares current output with baseline, checks hot/loose terminals, cleans safely, and records battery health.

lessons.title: Week 1 — Site survey, demand, and solar resource
lessons.briefing:
A solar system starts with a load audit, not a panel catalogue. List every appliance, its watts, hours per day, and surge current. Daily energy is watts × hours. Separate essential loads (clinic fridge, lights, router) from optional loads. Inspect the roof for orientation, shading from trees and water tanks, corrosion, wind exposure, access, and structural condition.

Use a sun-path app or repeated observation, but verify on site. One shaded cell can reduce a whole string. Decide whether the project is off-grid, grid-tied, or hybrid; each has different protection and legal requirements. Record cable routes and distances because voltage drop determines conductor size.

The survey report includes client needs, load table, photos, risks, proposed equipment location, and an initial single-line diagram. Do not promise “24-hour power” before calculating worst-month generation and storage.

lessons.title: Stop and steer: hydraulics, discs, suspension
lessons.titleSw: Simama na elekeza: hydraulics, discs, suspension
lessons.briefing:
Brakes convert motion to heat. The pedal moves a booster (vacuum or electric) then a tandem master cylinder. Fluid in two circuits (diagonal or front/rear split) goes through lines, often an ABS modulator, to calipers (disc) or wheel cylinders (drum). Pads clamp a disc; shoes expand in a drum. A leaking hose or boiling old fluid is a long pedal.

ABS does not create grip; it limits lock so you can still steer. If the ABS light is on, you still have foundation brakes — but the anatomy of the modulator and sensors is now in play.

The same corner holds the hub, bearing, disc, caliper bracket, steering arm, spring, and damper. A warped disc complaint is often a hub face or a sticking slide. A pull under braking can be a seized caliper, a collapsed hose, or alignment after a bent arm.

Steering: rack (or box), track rods, and geometry (toe, camber, caster). Suspension: spring supports the mass; damper controls the oscillation. Anatomy sites draw them together because a tyre only works when it is pointing and loaded correctly.
lessons.briefingSw: Pedal → booster → master → mistari → caliper au drum. ABS haizai grip. Koner moja ina disc, bearing, spring, damper, na steering arm.

exercises.prompt: A tandem master cylinder is used so that:
exercises.explanation: Legal dual-circuit design. A single leak must not empty the whole system.

options.text: One leak can still leave a second circuit

exercises.prompt: ABS is designed to:
exercises.explanation: Anti-lock. On some surfaces stopping distance can grow; control is the point.

options.text: Always shorten stopping on ice below foundation brakes
Limit lock so the driver can still steer

exercises.prompt: Disc brakes use a ___ to squeeze the pads.
exercises.explanation: Caliper. Slides and piston seals are service items.

exercises.prompt: Label the hydraulic path to the corner.
exercises.hint: Pressure starts at the master; clamp is at the disc.
exercises.explanation: Master, caliper, and the corner that holds the tyre down.

exercises.prompt: Long pedal after a hose job, no warning lamp. First anatomy check?
exercises.explanation: Open the system, you own the bleed. Then look for a drip you created.

options.text: Bleed and inspect for a leak or leftover air in the open circuit

lessons.title: Cooling and lubrication loops
lessons.briefing:
Combustion heat would seize the engine without two loops. Coolant carries heat from jackets in the block and head to the radiator. Air through the core (ram air + fans) dumps that heat. The thermostat holds temperature until the engine is warm, then opens. The pump (belt or electric) moves the liquid. An expansion tank gives the system a place to grow and a place to bleed.

Pressure (cap rating) raises the boiling point. Test only to spec. Plastic tanks on aluminium cores fail at the crimp; copper/brass can be soldered. Blocked tubes make cold vertical stripes on a hot core.

Oil is a film, not just a level on the dipstick. The pump picks up from the sump, through a pickup screen, to galleries, bearings, and often a cooler or filter bypass. Low level, aeration, or a blocked pickup is a bearing death sentence. Coolant in oil or oil in coolant is a shared-wall failure: gasket, cracked head, or cracked block.

Bleed after any open repair. An air lock at the head or heater matrix looks like a “bad thermostat”. Fans and shrouds are part of the anatomy — a missing shroud is a highway overheat waiting in Nairobi traffic.
lessons.briefingSw: Coolant inachukua joto kwenda radiator. Thermostat inafungua baada ya joto. Pump inasukuma. Mafuta ni filamu kwenye bearings. Hewa kwenye mfumo inaiga thermostat mbaya.

exercises.prompt: The part that keeps coolant in the engine until it is warm is the:
exercises.explanation: Thermostat. Stuck closed overheats; stuck open never warms and wastes fuel.

exercises.prompt: Oil’s primary job at the crank bearings is:
exercises.explanation: Pressure and viscosity make the film. Level and pump health matter.

options.text: A pressurised film that prevents metal-to-metal contact

exercises.prompt: Heat leaves the coolant as air passes through the ___.
exercises.explanation: Radiator core + fans + shroud.

exercises.prompt: Label the cooling loop.
exercises.hint: Heat exchanger at the nose, valve in the engine, jackets in the metal.
exercises.explanation: Radiator rejects heat; thermostat times flow; jackets collect it.

exercises.prompt: After a hose change the dash gauge climbs in traffic. First anatomy move?
exercises.explanation: Open cooling systems trap air. Bleed and prove fans before you buy a pump.

options.text: Bleed, confirm level/cap, fans, then flow — before parts roulette
Add engine oil to the tank

lessons.title: Drivetrain: clutch, gears, shafts, differential
lessons.briefing:
The drivetrain is everything after the crank flange: flywheel or flexplate, clutch or torque converter, gearbox, then shafts to a differential that splits torque to the wheels and allows them to turn at different speeds in a corner.

FWD: transaxle in the engine bay, short driveshafts with CV joints to the front hubs. RWD: gearbox, propshaft with U-joints, rear axle/diff, then half-shafts. 4WD/AWD adds a transfer case or coupling and a second axle.

Gear ratios multiply torque. A slipping clutch smells and revs without road speed. A failed CV clicks on lock. A worn U-joint clunks on take-up. A locked diff or a broken spider gear is a corner hop or a bang.

Do not confuse drivetrain vibration with engine misfire: road-speed vs engine-speed is the anatomy test. Support the engine/gearbox on the correct mounts before you chase a “vibration at 80”.
lessons.briefingSw: Baada ya crank: flywheel, clutch au converter, gearbox, shafts, diff. FWD ina transaxle. RWD ina propshaft. Gia zinazidisha torque. CV inabofya kwenye lock.

exercises.prompt: A differential exists so that:
exercises.explanation: Without a diff, a driven axle fights itself in a corner.

options.text: Both wheels must always spin at one speed
Driven wheels can rotate at different speeds in a turn

exercises.prompt: FWD power typically leaves the gearbox through:
exercises.explanation: Front-wheel drive uses short CV shafts.

options.text: A long timber propshaft to a rear beam
Driveshafts with CV joints to the front hubs

exercises.prompt: The assembly that lets driven wheels turn at different speeds is the ___.
exercises.explanation: Differential / final drive.

exercises.prompt: Label how torque leaves the engine.
exercises.hint: Box, then shaft, then split to the wheels.
exercises.explanation: Gearbox, shaft, differential.

exercises.prompt: Clicking on full lock after a pothole, no engine misfire. Anatomy target?
exercises.explanation: Classic CV. Confirm boot, play, and grease before you rebuild an engine.

lessons.title: Electrical nervous system: battery, alternator, loads
lessons.titleSw: Mfumo wa umeme: betri, alternator, loads
lessons.briefing:
Think of the electrical system as a nervous system on a cutaway layer: battery (stored energy), starter (cranking load), alternator (running generation), distribution (cables, fusible links, boxes), controllers (ECU, body modules), and loads (lamps, pumps, ignition, infotainment).

The battery must crank and buffer. The alternator must cover running loads plus recharge. A “dead battery” after night parking can be a parasitic draw or a charging fault — measure voltage and current; do not guess.

Earths are half the circuit. A painted earth or a chewed loom at the hatch hinge is a living anatomy lesson. Fuses protect wires, not your schedule: a repeated fuse is a short, not a market for a bigger fuse.

Starting path: ignition/enable → starter relay → solenoid → pinion to ring gear. Charging path: belt → alternator → output cable → battery positive, with the ECU sometimes commanding the field.

Never work live on an SRS airbag circuit. Disconnect and wait as the data says. Anatomy includes what you must not probe.
lessons.briefingSw: Betri inahifadhi. Starter inazungusha. Alternator inazalisha injini ikiwaka. Earth ni nusu ya mzunguko. Fuse inalinda waya, si kazi yako.

exercises.prompt: While the engine runs, the main source of electrical energy should be the:
exercises.explanation: Alternator (or DC-DC on some hybrids). The battery buffers.

exercises.prompt: A fuse that blows again after you “upgrade” the rating is telling you:
exercises.explanation: The fuse is a designed weak point. Find the fault.

options.text: There is still a short or overload — fix the circuit

exercises.prompt: The machine that converts belt rotation into charging current is the ___.
exercises.hint: Generator on the front of the engine.
exercises.explanation: Alternator. Belt, pulley, regulator, and output cable are part of the same anatomy.

exercises.prompt: Label the charging and cranking parts.
exercises.explanation: Battery stores, alternator generates, starter cranks.

exercises.prompt: Cranks slowly, lights dim, 11.2 V at rest. Anatomy-first action?
exercises.explanation: Low rest voltage is a battery or parasitic story. Prove charge next.

options.text: Test/charge/replace the battery and prove the charging circuit before more parts

lessons.title: Engine cutaway: air, fuel, spark, bottom end
lessons.briefing:
The engine is a pump that burns a mixture and turns heat into crank rotation. Vocational maps split: top end (head, valves, cam, intake, exhaust, ignition or injectors) and bottom end (block, pistons, rods, crank, sump).

Four-stroke order: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Spark-ignition (petrol) lights a compressed mix. Compression-ignition (diesel) injects into hot air. Wrong fuel, wrong glow/spark, or no air (blocked filter / collapsed hose) all look like “no power”.

Air path: filter → meter/MAF if fitted → throttle or diesel intake → manifold → valve → cylinder. Exhaust: valve → manifold → turbo if fitted → after-treatment → silencer. A boost leak after a turbo is a power complaint with a black or clean tailpipe depending on fueling.

Bottom-end noises and oil pressure are not “add thicker oil and release”. Low pressure, mayonnaise, coolant in oil, or white smoke send you to the cooling and sealing lesson next — the systems share the head gasket and jackets.

Always isolate: fuel delivery, spark/glow, compression, timing, air. Anatomy prevents swapping a coil when the timing chain has jumped.
lessons.briefingSw: Injini ni pampu ya moto. Top end: kichwa, valves, intake, exhaust. Bottom end: block, pistoni, crank. Four-stroke: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Tenganisha hewa, mafuta, cheche, compression.

exercises.prompt: The crankshaft lives in the:
exercises.explanation: Pistons and rods turn the crank in the block. The head holds valves.

exercises.prompt: A diesel that will not start after sitting in the cold is missing heat for:
exercises.hint: No spark plugs on a diesel.
exercises.explanation: Glow plugs / compression heat. Petrol needs a spark; diesel needs hot air.

exercises.prompt: The four strokes are intake, compression, power, and ___.
exercises.explanation: Intake–compression–power–exhaust.

exercises.prompt: Place the labels on this engine cutaway.
exercises.hint: Top end, bottom end, rotating assembly.
exercises.explanation: Head above, pistons in the block, crank at the bottom.

exercises.prompt: A 1.5 petrol has a misfire on cylinder 2. Anatomy-first checks?
exercises.explanation: Localise to the hole before you replace a used engine.

options.text: Spark/injector, compression/leak-down, then timing — on that hole

lessons.title: Whole-car map: body, cabin, chassis
lessons.titleSw: Ramani ya gari: body, cabin, chasi
lessons.briefing:
Car-anatomy sites start with a map, not a single bolt. A vehicle is a carrying structure plus systems hung on it. The chassis (or subframe + body-in-white on a unibody car) is the skeleton: rails, cross-members, and mounting points that locate the engine, suspension, steering, and fuel tank. The body/cabin is the occupant cell and crash structure. Doors, glass, and trim are not the frame.

Unibody cars combine body and structure. Body-on-frame pickups still have a ladder frame you can point to. Either way, loads travel: engine torque into mounts, braking into knuckles and subframe, pothole loads into springs and then the body. If a mount or rail is rusted, “just replace the part” is not a diagnosis.

Walk a car the way a cutaway is layered: engine bay (power + cooling + charging), cabin (controls, HVAC, restraints), floor (exhaust, fuel, brake/fuel lines), corners (hub, bearing, brake, spring, damper, steering arm), rear (tank, spare, driveline).

Kenya workshop habit: look for accident pull, wet battery trays, crushed sills, and missing undertrays before you chase a noise. The map tells you which system can make that symptom.

lessons.briefing:
Compost needs carbon-rich browns, nitrogen-rich greens, moisture like a wrung sponge, oxygen, and time. Exclude batteries, glass, plastics, treated timber, meat where the system cannot manage it, and human waste unless a specialised process exists. Business records include input weight, recovery rate, labour, transport, buyer price, rejects, and PPE costs. Community benefit is real only if the enterprise is safe, lawful, and solvent.

lessons.briefing:
Safe water can become unsafe after treatment. Inspect the source for latrines uphill, animal access, flood paths, cracked aprons, and standing water. Collect with clean containers that are not dipped by dirty cups. Household treatment may use boiling, approved chlorine dose/contact time, or filtration—follow public-health guidance and product instructions.

Chlorine is not guessed by smell. Dose depends on concentration, turbidity, and volume. Very cloudy water may need settling and filtration first. Store treated water in a covered, narrow-neck container with a tap. Do not put hands or cups inside.

A sanitary inspection records hazards and corrective actions. Water testing and health authorities confirm microbiological safety; a clear-looking spring is not proof.

lessons.briefing:
Sanitation breaks faecal–oral transmission. Inspect the slab for cracks, privacy and safety, flies/odour, a washable surface, a child-safe opening, and distance from water sources according to local public-health rules. A full, collapsing, or flood-prone pit is an emergency to isolate and escalate—not a place for a trainee to enter.

Handwashing stations need reliable water, soap or approved alternative, drainage that does not form a mosquito pool, and a design children and persons with disabilities can use. Tippy taps work only if refilled and repaired. Assign responsibility.

lessons.title: Weld defects and visual inspection
lessons.briefing:
Visual inspection is the first NDT. Look at profile, undercut, overlap, craters, and spatter. Undercut is a groove melted into the parent metal along the toe — it is a stress raiser. Porosity is gas holes from contamination, long arc, or damp flux. Slag inclusions happen when you do not chip and brush between passes. Lack of fusion is a cold joint that looks joined until it peels.

Cracks are never “just cosmetic”. Stop. Report. Do not peen a crack to hide it. For many student butts, the repair is grind to sound metal and re-weld, not a third pass over dirt.

Measure throat and legs with a gauge if you have one. A pretty ripple on an undersize fillet still fails. Parent metal thickness and the drawing decide the size, not your eye from two metres.

Write defects in the log with the cause: “undercut — current high / travel slow at the toe.” That sentence is how you improve, and how assessors see that you understand metallurgy at craft level.

lessons.title: Oxy-fuel, leaks, and simple fabrication
lessons.briefing:
Oxy-acetylene is still taught for cutting, heating, and braze-welding. Cylinders stay chained. Open oxygen slowly. Acetylene: keep cylinders upright, and know the 15 psi (about 1 bar) working-pressure caution taught in class — follow the college chart. Flashback arrestors and correct hose colours (red fuel, blue oxygen in many Kenyan shops — confirm local standard) are not decorations.

Leak test with approved solution, never a flame. An icy fitting can mean a leaking gas expanding. If you smell acetylene: shut cylinders, no sparks, ventilate, and fetch the instructor.

Fabrication: measure twice, square with a builder’s square or 3-4-5, tack opposite corners, check, then weld. Distortion is controlled by sequence, not by hoping. Cut with a clean piercing method off the line, then run the cut; slag on the floor is hot.

A square gate that is diamond-shaped after welding was tacked out of square. Fit-up is most of fabrication.

lessons.title: Week 5 — GMAW / MIG: gas, wire, and set-up
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 5 — GMAW/MIG: gesi, waya, na set-up
lessons.briefing:
CDACC welding Level 5 includes GMAW (MIG) as a core separate from MMA. The electrode is a continuously fed solid wire. Shielding gas (often CO₂ or Ar/CO₂ mix for steel — follow the WPS) displaces air so the puddle does not nitride and porosity. No gas, or a blocked nozzle, looks like a “bad machine”. Clean the nozzle and contact tip; a fused tip is a feed fault, not a new inverter.

Set voltage (or “trim”) and wire-speed together. Too little heat: ropey, lack of fusion. Too much: burn-through on thin sheet. Stick-out (contact tip to work) is typically about 10–15 mm as taught — long stick-out cools the arc and increases spatter. Earth clamp on clean metal, same as MMA. Push (forehand) for flatter beads on many steel fillets; drag if the WPS says so for a given transfer mode.

Transfer modes you should name: short-circuit (thin sheet, more spatter), globular, spray (needs enough current and usually argon-rich mix). Do not run spray on 1 mm sheet. PPE still includes a filter; MIG is an arc. Spats burn through synthetic shirts — leather or flame-resistant cotton.

Practical: fillet on 6 mm, then a butt on 2–3 mm with backing as specified. Assessors mark gas on before the strike, and a bead that fuses both toes.

lessons.title: Joints, electrodes, and MMA setup
lessons.briefing:
MMA/SMAW (stick) is the common polytechnic process. Joint types: butt (edges in one plane), lap (overlap), T-fillet, and corner. A fillet sits in the included angle; its size is the leg length, not how pretty the ripples look. Clean mill scale, rust, and oil from the joint. A dirty joint is porosity waiting to happen.

Electrode diameter and current are paired. A typical starting point many trainers use: roughly 30–40 A per millimetre of electrode diameter, then tune to the puddle. Too cold: the slag fights you and the bead sits high. Too hot: undercut and burn-through on thin plate. Electrode angle and arc length (about the core diameter) matter as much as the dial.

Strike on the joint or on a scrap, not on the bench. Travel speed should leave a bead about twice the core diameter for many pad welds — follow the WPS or job card. Stop, chip, and inspect between runs on a multi-pass butt. Interpass temperature matters on thicker plate; do not freeze a second pass onto black cold slag.

Store electrodes dry. Damp rutile/basic rods give hydrogen cracks and porosity. If the oven is required, use it.

lessons.title: Arc safety, PPE, and the bay
lessons.titleSw: Usalama wa arc, PPE, na bay
lessons.briefing:
Welding is a high-risk trade. Shade 10–13 filters (follow electrode and process), leather gloves, apron or jacket, and closed boots are not optional. Cotton under-layers beat melting synthetics. Screens protect the next trainee. Chipping slag without eye protection is how “welder’s flash” and metal-in-eye cases fill the clinic every term.

Treat cylinders, cables, and the workpiece as a system. Isolate the machine when changing electrodes if the procedure requires it; never coil cables around your body. The workpiece clamp must be on clean metal, not a painted bench edge that arcs randomly. Ventilate: zinc on galvanised steel produces fumes that make you ill; grind coatings off in a controlled way and extract.

Housekeeping is part of safety: no water on the floor around MMA sets, no oily rags by grinders, fire extinguisher known and unblocked. Hot work needs a watcher if the college rule says so. Never weld on a closed tank that held fuel.

Assessors watch helmet-down before the strike, not after you see the puddle. That habit is the first competence.

lessons.title: Week 6 — GTAW / TIG: tungsten, gas, and cleanliness
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 6 — TIG: tungsten, gesi, na usafi
lessons.briefing:
TIG (GTAW) is a CDACC core because stainless tanks, food plant, and thin aluminium (where taught) need a clean, controllable arc. The tungsten is not consumed as filler — you add a separate rod. Shielding is usually argon. Contaminated tungsten (dipped in the puddle) is reground; a dirty tip wanders and spatters tungsten inclusions into the weld — a test fail.

Grind tungsten along its length (not across) to a point for DC on steel/stainless; AC on aluminium uses a different balance/blob as taught. Polarity: DCEN (electrode negative) is common for steel TIG. Gas post-flow protects the cooling tungsten and the crater. No post-flow = oxidised tip and a sugared stainless root.

Cleanliness is the process: stainless brushed with a stainless-only brush, joints degreased, no mill scale if the WPS forbids it. Filler is added to the leading edge of the puddle, not stabbed through the arc onto cold metal. Foot pedal or torch amp control lets you taper out to avoid a crater crack.

PPE: TIG is still UV. Thin gloves for dexterity but cover skin. Practical: autogenous fusion on stainless sheet, then a fillet with filler. Assessors watch gas pre-flow and a shiny, not black, stainless face.
lessons.briefingSw: Tungsten si filler — ongeza fimbo. Argon. Kama tungsten ichafuliwa, saga upya. DCEN kwa chuma. Post-flow. Stainless brush tofauti. Usichome crater. Uso wa stainless uwe shiny.

lessons.briefing:
Weld testing is a CDACC core (visual plus mechanical/NDT introduction). Start with visual: size, profile, undercut, overlap, porosity, slag, incomplete fusion, cracks, and spatter. Use a fillet gauge. A pretty ripple with undercut at the toe fails. Lighting and slag fully chipped — you cannot inspect through slag.

Destructive tests in college: nick-break, face/root bend, and sometimes a macro etch. Bends reveal lack of fusion that visual missed. Non-destructive: dye penetrant (surface cracks), MPI on ferritic steel, and ultrasonics/radiography in industry. You will not run a gamma source without a licence; you must know when to call that test.

Acceptance is against a code or the college WPS, not against “it held my weight”. Repair: grind to sound metal, re-weld, re-test. Peening cracks closed or filling with silicone is malpractice.

Portfolio: a visual report with sketches, a bend result, and a sentence on why a cracked tandem-trailer hitch must not leave the bay. That is professional welding, not hobby art.
